newsitem.title: ITALY: N.Korean defector says will defect or die--S.Korea.
newsitem.headline: N.Korean defector says will defect or die--S.Korea.

text.p: Hwang Jang-yop, the leading North Korean ideologue seeking asylum in the south, has said he will die in Seoul's Beijing mission if his request is not granted, South Korea's embassy in Rome said on Friday.
Hwang told a senior South Korean official in Beijing "I will die here if my determination to go to South Korea cannot be realised," according to a statement issued by the embassy but datelined Seoul.
"I want to make it clear that South Korea is the place where I want to go, and I will not go to any third country," the statement quoted him as saying.
Hwang spent his third day with an aide in the consular office of Seoul's Beijing embassy on Friday as China urged calm while it negotiated with South Korea on his fate.

China warned of a drawn-out standoff after it was dragged unwillingly into the squabble over Hwang between the two Koreas, bitter enemies for half a century. It is faced with making a decision that must anger either an old communist comrade or a new friend and wealthy investor.
The embassy statement said Seoul's foreign ministry had issued a statement on Thursday hand-written by Hwang.

It quoted Hwang's note as saying he had "agonised with himself repeatedly before making the decision to leave the North and go south to consult with personages in the South on ways to rescue our nation from misfortune".
Hwang, referring to North Korea, asked: "Are those people in their right mind when they claim loudly to have built an ideal society, while workers and farmers are starving?" it said.
"My remaining life will not be long. I am a failed man in politics," the statement quoted Hwang's note as saying.
"I don't have a slightest intention to take a share in any one side. I only wish to give help to south-north relations and unification until the last minute of my life."

Hwang was the chief architect of North Korea's national ideology of Juche, a doctrine of fanatical self-reliance, and his defection would be a major blow for Pyongyang, already suffering from severe food shortages and a tottering economy.

Korea was divided at the end of World War Two and the truce which ended the 1950-53 war between North and South Korea and their respective allies has never been followed by a peace treaty. China fought on North Korea's side.
